attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, stated as his conclusion.

semantics.note: Causal is the right kind. But the proposition weakens 'far more' to 'more', drops 'antagonistic approach to doing business', and turns 'needs right now' into 'actual need', which loses the time scope. The contract keeps all of these, so the scoring is not affected.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary: NVIDIA-induced early or excess purchasing explains substantially more apparent demand than current needs do. Asking for causal and market-level comparison evidence suits a claim that it is 'proven'. No margin is invented.

evidence.note: CoreWeave 10-Q (May 2026). Customer contracts specify NVIDIA, and it says it orders only what it needs. This covers one buyer and has no market-wide or utilization data, so it leans against the claim but cannot refute it.

NVIDIA 10-Q discloses capacity-backstop and financing arrangements and a demand risk. Supplier support is relevant but does not show deliberate channel stuffing or how big its effect is compared with real need.
TechSpot report on GPUs warehoused because power is short. Amazon calls this 'best business practice' (an interested party). It neither shows nor rules out NVIDIA pressure.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no contracts, communications or independent findings showing deliberate NVIDIA pressure. It also has no market-level comparison of induced versus operational demand. The counterevidence (CoreWeave's ordering statement, Amazon's explanation) is limited or self-interested and does not refute the mechanism across the market. The claim is checked but not settled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own post.

semantics.note: Faithful to the words, including 'vast majority'. It is a firm present-tense claim, so observation is the right kind, even though 'economic sense' is an evaluative phrase.

contract.note: The speaker gave no test. Reading it as 'delivery costs exceed customer payments' fits the context, which is about customers burning many times their subscription price in tokens. Weighting by spending and using Q3 2026 are evaluator choices, but reasonable and not stretched against him.

evidence.note: Cognition pricing page from April 2026, before the target quarter. It describes quotas and billing at model cost, but gives no realized margins and no market coverage. It is a company disclosure from a single firm.

reviews.rationale: The only evidence is one company's pricing announcement from before the target period. Nothing in the packet is representative, spending-weighted Q3 2026 data matching AI service payments to delivery costs. Neither the support nor the contradiction condition can be assessed.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The flat chain of 'will' consequences after an 'if' is a conditional forecast. Merging the nested conditionals into one antecedent is acceptable. No horizon was stated.

contract.note: In context, 'customer' means a data-center tenant whose trouble hits collateral backing data-center bonds. The contract widens this to any indirect cloud buyer so it can mark the condition met using Character.ai's arrears to vendors. The packet admits the narrower reading leaves the antecedent unverified, and the link between the payables and compute vendors is inferred.

evidence.note: Character.ai announces Chapter 11 (12 Oct 2026). This is a company disclosure about the bankruptcy, not about payment to data-center suppliers or the chain of consequences.

Secondhand report on a motion admitting late payments to critical vendors. The report says the motion does not connect this to the listed Google or DigitalOcean payables. At most it bears on the antecedent, not the outcome.

reviews.rationale: Read fairly, the antecedent is a data-center tenant unable to pay. The packet does not establish that: Character.ai's vendor arrears are not tied to data-center capacity. With the antecedent unknown, the conditional is not scored. Even on the contract's broad reading, there is no completed chain or conclusive event and no deadline, so nothing could be scored yet.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Their' does refer to the Asian companies named just before. The target list leaves out Kioxia, SMBC and MUFG, and the proposition drops the 'like the American markets' comparison. These are minor. It is a firm causal claim.

contract.note: Reading 'in perpetuity' as indefinite-growth expectations that materially explain valuation premiums is an ordinary reading of hyperbolic but firm language. Choosing the publication date as the valuation state is a reasonable convention.

evidence.note: TSMC call transcript: management calls demand 'extremely robust' and gives a growth outlook to 2029. This is management's expectation, not investor belief in growth forever.

Valuation publisher, 19 Oct. TSMC's P/E is below the peer median and analysts price a 2027 growth multiple. These finite assumptions hint at no perpetual premium for TSMC but do not show what drives market beliefs.

Secondary summary of an unverified BofA note: Samsung and SK Hynix at about 3x forward P/E, more than 50% below June highs. This leans against perpetual-growth pricing for the memory makers, but it covers two companies and the original is unverified.

reviews.rationale: No item measures investor growth horizons or isolates them from other valuation drivers across the named companies. The memory-maker multiples (e3) and TSMC's discount to peers (e2) point against perpetual-growth pricing, but they are secondary or model-based and incomplete. They do not meet either condition for the whole set.
